competencies.title: Results and next steps
competencies.meaning: Use an observed result to decide whether to finish, make a targeted correction and check again, investigate differently, or hand back an unresolved decision. Assess the connection from a result to the action it causes.
competencies.evidence: Follow one independent task from its applicable pass conditions to the actual returned observation, the action taken because of it, and the next observed state. Read command output, product observations, review findings, or evaluator feedback together with the correction, rerun, and completion report. For delegated work, trace the finding to its responsible executor and back to the combined result. Attribute the person's adopted instructions separately from AI's own execution. A check command without its output, a saved rule, or an executor's success message alone does not establish this connection.
competencies.high: The observed state controls what happens next, and the episode reaches an endpoint supported by that state. AI uses a failure's diagnostic to correct the relevant cause, obtains a fresh result, and chooses the next action from it. A passing first attempt can lead directly to completion; no failure or extra round is required. Example: the project's report comparison finds missing refund rows. AI corrects the exclusion rule, generates the report again, reads the matching totals, and finishes. If the comparison already matches, it finishes from that result.
competencies.medium: A result causes a relevant action, but an inspected completed episode leaves that action's effect unconfirmed. Example: AI reads the project's refund mismatch and changes the exclusion rule, then ends the task saying the repair is ready without generating the report again. The result influenced the correction, but no observed result closes that correction path.
competencies.low: An available result is disregarded or contradicted by the next action. Example: the report comparison still shows missing refunds, but AI marks the report complete, or keeps changing typography despite diagnostics identifying omitted rows. Repeating the same failed action without a changed hypothesis, changed state, or a supported transient-retry reason also demonstrates a broken connection. An unresolved failure reported honestly is not Low by itself.
competencies.whyItHelps: Feedback helps when it changes a decision. A correction linked to the diagnostic addresses the observed problem, and a fresh result establishes whether that correction worked. Recognizing a passing endpoint also prevents extra work after the required outcome is established.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when a task returns a result that can inform a next action. Credit an applied standing instruction, an adopted AI procedure, or appropriate delegation; the person need not personally run the check or write the fix. Judge check validity and coverage under Testing & Evals rather than awarding those properties again here.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents
sources.note: The evaluator-optimizer pattern uses explicit criteria and useful evaluation feedback to guide revision. The agent pattern obtains environmental results to assess progress and can stop at completion. Adopted mechanism: observations determine revision or completion; adding evaluators or iterations is not itself evidence of improvement.

sources.title: obra/superpowers — Verification Before Completion
sources.note: Its gate reads actual output before making a status claim and checks a delegated executor's result. Adopted mechanism: the reported endpoint follows observed evidence, including a fresh result after a repair, rather than a completion message.

sources.title: pstack — Fix Root Causes
sources.note: Reproduce, inspect actual state, and trace a symptom to the first wrong decision. It warns that swallowed errors and inappropriate retries can hide the fault. Adopted mechanism: direct corrective action at the supported cause without erasing the failure signal.

competencies.title: Execution recovery
competencies.meaning: Let AI identify and resolve routine obstacles that prevent work or checks from running, within the task's authority. When safe recovery is unavailable, stop with the evidence and exact assistance needed, preserving completed work for resumption.
competencies.evidence: Inspect the failed command or unavailable dependency, relevant environment and state checks, the diagnosis, the authorized recovery or changed approach, and an actual rerun. Read applicable retry, permission, and resource limits and what happened when they were reached. For a handback, inspect the blocked action, completed results, unresolved scope, required access or decision, and any later resumption. Determine whether AI investigated accessible facts itself or repeatedly made the person relay diagnostics it could obtain.
competencies.high: AI collects the available diagnostic, distinguishes a recoverable execution problem from a permission or decision boundary, and resolves a routine authorized problem without requiring the person to supply discoverable facts. It reruns the affected operation before proceeding. When recovery needs unavailable authority or an unresolved human decision, it applies a bounded stop condition and provides a usable handback. Example: the project's local verifier cannot start under the selected runtime. AI reads the repository's runtime requirement, selects an already installed compatible runtime, and confirms startup and the resumed check. If the remaining staging comparison is denied, it stops that path, identifies the needed read role, and retains the confirmed local results.
competencies.medium: AI detects the execution obstacle and takes a relevant recovery or stopping action, but the observed handling leaves avoidable work with the person or loses the route to resumption. Example: AI identifies the project's wrong runtime but makes the person repeatedly inspect the locally accessible version and rerun the command, or stops at the staging denial with only 'access blocked' and no indication of the comparison still needed. Do not count a genuinely necessary access grant or product decision as avoidable human work.
competencies.low: An inspected obstacle leads to blind continuation, an unauthorized recovery, or a misleading state. Example: AI repeats the same denied staging request after the applicable stop condition, disables the access check to proceed, kills an unrelated process to obtain a port, or reports the blocked comparison as passed. A retry that learns something new or responds to an established transient failure is not blind repetition.
competencies.whyItHelps: Execution failures can prevent useful feedback from being produced at all. Diagnosing accessible state and repairing the relevant environment restores that path. Bounded recovery preserves authority and resources, while a precise handback lets the responsible person unblock the specific remaining action without reconstructing the whole task.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when an actual execution obstacle, interruption, or resource boundary requires recovery, stopping, or resumption. An appropriate evidence-backed stop can be High even though the blocked operation remains unverified. This level evaluates handling of the obstacle, not successful verification of the blocked behavior.

sources.title: addyosmani/agent-skills — Debugging and Error Recovery
sources.note: Preserves failure evidence, localizes the affected layer, and distinguishes build configuration, dependencies, environment, and external-service causes. Adopted mechanism: diagnose the actual execution obstacle before selecting a recovery, then resume from verification rather than suppressing the failure.

sources.title: obra/superpowers — Systematic Debugging
sources.note: Reads errors, reproduces behavior, inspects configuration across component boundaries, tests a specific hypothesis, and changes course after unsuccessful fixes. Adopted mechanism: evidence-guided recovery and a stopping boundary. The source's particular attempt count is not adopted as a universal scoring requirement.

sources.title: pstack — Create a verification skill
sources.note: Investigates repository facts before asking the user and includes a read-only instance health check. Cleanup removes only instances the run created and preserves evidence. Adopted mechanism: investigate routine setup independently and recover within the owned environment.

competencies.title: Workflow maintenance
competencies.meaning: Reuse a working result-to-action procedure in comparable tasks without additional user intervention each time. Keep its diagnostic routes, responsible executor, recovery limits, and stopping decisions aligned with actual work, retaining or repairing the existing mechanism as evidence warrants.
competencies.evidence: Connect the executed procedure to a separate later applicable task, its automatic invocation or default AI use, the returned results reaching the responsible AI, and the actions those results caused. Inspect observed drift or repeated ineffective handling, any revision to result routing or decision rules, and actual operation afterward. A hook, saved skill, scheduled job, or instruction alone proves neither invocation nor an effective loop. Do not infer a broken route solely because no later run is available.
competencies.high: Later comparable work follows the reusable loop without the person having to request verification or relay accessible results again. Its results actually reach the executor that can act, and evidence supports retaining the working route or fixing demonstrated drift. Any changed route is exercised before claiming its effect. Example: the project' completion procedure runs its existing verifier and returns diagnostics to the implementing AI. A later export change uses that route without additional user intervention; an observed failure reaches AI, AI repairs it, and the new result determines completion. If later checks pass and the route remains suitable, deliberate retention meets the same level. Only branches actually reached need to be demonstrated.
competencies.medium: A reusable route operates in later work, but an observed connection still depends on repeated human prompting or relay, or a demonstrated procedure revision is applied without checking its intended effect despite available results. Example: the project automatically runs its verifier, yet the implementing AI never receives its failed output until the person pastes it. This is a partially connected loop even though the verification job itself works.
competencies.low: A known recurring routing or decision failure remains active in comparable work without an effective response. Example: repeated runs show that the project records failed exports in an unread log and still ends as complete. The next run follows the same route and again omits the failure from its decision. Repeatedly adding additional user interventions while the demonstrated broken connection remains unchanged does not establish maintenance.
competencies.whyItHelps: A reusable connection carries successful feedback handling into the next task, reducing the need for the person to restart it manually. Actual reuse reveals stale assumptions, missing result delivery, or limits that no longer fit. Repairing that specific connection preserves useful work and avoids creating competing procedures.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when comparable work recurs or an existing reusable loop has a genuine upkeep opportunity. High requires observed use without additional user intervention for each task, whether a harness invokes the loop or AI applies an adopted standing procedure. Personal judgment need not be automated. Do not prescribe an extra run, hook, schedule, skill, or procedural change merely to create scoring evidence.

sources.title: pstack — Maintain a verification skill
sources.note: Distinguishes procedure drift, harness gaps, and product regressions; checks instance health after surprising behavior; reruns harness fixes; and reports clean, changed, or blocked outcomes. Adopted mechanism: maintain the existing feedback route against actual execution and preserve honest outcomes.

sources.title: pstack — Encode Lessons in Structure
sources.note: Recurring corrections should become an appropriate executable check or structural mechanism where possible. Lessons that require judgment remain guidance with a concrete example. Adopted mechanism: replace repeated manual reminders with an applied reusable connection when the lesson can be operationalized.

boundaries: Testing & Evals assesses whether a check reaches the relevant behavior, discriminates success from failure, and runs repeatably. Feedback Loops assesses what the returned result causes next. A valid check that runs automatically can still feed a broken loop if its result never reaches the responsible AI. Do not award check quality or case coverage twice.

Human Steering assesses how the person judges proposals, redirects work, and reconsiders earlier decisions using evidence. An AI-controlled recovery or completion decision supports Feedback Loops without proving that the person interpreted the evidence. Necessary human approval of a real decision or permission is compatible with a strong loop.

Task Mapping assesses assignments, dependencies, handoffs, and integration. Feedback Loops follows a returned failure into correction or escalation and back into an observed result. Multiple agents are optional.

Tool Integration assesses whether a reusable procedure works as a tool and remains usable. This dimension assesses its result delivery, decision routes, bounded recovery, and effective reuse. Saving the same procedure does not separately establish Memory & Knowledge credit.

Results guide the next step covers action on an obtained work result. Fix what blocks execution covers an obstacle preventing work or a check from running reliably. Keep the loop working requires a separate reuse or upkeep opportunity. One incident must not be split into several competencies merely to reward the same corrective action.

No failure, permission denial, interruption, repeated mistake, or changed procedure is required. Assess only observed opportunities and reached branches. Do not infer Low from a short record, an unobserved later run, or an unresolved external blocker.

Retries must have a diagnostic purpose or a supported transient-recovery reason and respect applicable limits. Never reward endless retries, suppressed failed checks, widened permissions, unauthorized side effects, or claiming blocked work complete. Preserve successful evidence when resuming unless changed inputs require rechecking.

example.notice: Illustrative output example, not evidence from this assessment.
example.summary: In the project, the refund mismatch changed AI's next action, and a fresh report comparison supported completion. the project ran its verifier on later export work, but its failed result still needed you to relay it before AI responded; connect that existing output to the responsible AI and inspect the next ordinary run.
example.expanded: Superpowers' evidence-before-completion gate supports checking the result after a repair; the project sequence shows that connection in action. Pstack's upkeep guidance supports diagnosing whether a problem is in the harness or product before changing the procedure; the project record establishes a missing delivery step, so repair that connection and confirm that the next relevant output changes AI's action. Neither a saved instruction nor an automatic job alone establishes that the full loop works.

competencies.title: User workflow testing
competencies.meaning: Establish what the affected product actually does by exercising its real user or operator entry point and inspecting the required outcome. Manual verification can fully demonstrate this practice.
competencies.evidence: Connect the requirement and affected revision to the running environment, actions or inputs, observed results, and the person or delegated evaluator who inspected them. Read interaction records, command output, response bodies, screenshots, saved artifacts, or persisted state as appropriate. Identify the required components and which parts were real, simulated, or unavailable. A launch, passing build, internal-function test, test name, or completion message alone does not establish the user outcome.
competencies.high: Exercises the affected version through the relevant real entry point in an appropriate test environment and checks the promised outcome, including a relevant side effect when that is part of the requirement. The observation distinguishes success from the failure at issue; a manual run or appropriately delegated run can qualify. Example: for the project's rescheduling change, someone opens an appointment in the running app, changes and saves its time, then reopens it and inspects the stored time. A run that reveals the wrong time is also effective verification of that failure; it does not establish that the feature is fixed.
competencies.medium: Runs a relevant part of the real workflow and inspects a meaningful result, but leaves an identified required outcome outside the check. Example: the project's edit form accepts a new time and displays a success message, but no check establishes the saved time after reopening, although persistence is required. Describe the confirmed portion and the remaining gap without inferring a product defect.
competencies.low: The observed verification or acceptance episode substitutes a build, static inspection, an AI assertion, or an unrelated check for execution of the required user behavior. Example: the project's save-and-reopen fix is marked functionally verified solely because compilation passed, despite the applicable requirement to exercise persistence.
competencies.whyItHelps: The user reaches a feature through a chain of interactions and connected components. Observing the required end state can reveal a failure that an isolated check or a successful startup cannot distinguish. It also makes the conclusion specific to the path and environment that were actually exercised.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the work changes behavior that a user, operator, API caller, CLI user, or library consumer needs to rely on. Use that surface's genuine public entry point; a graphical interface is unnecessary for a CLI or library. A supported sandbox or service test mode can be appropriate. If a required external step cannot safely run, preserve the unverified boundary; do not demand an unsafe live transaction. Credit the person's adopted procedure or delegation when the connected run and inspected result are visible; do not attribute an AI's independent omission to the person without evidence.

sources.title: Best Practices — Test user-visible behavior
sources.note: Recommends checking behavior as an end user sees and interacts with it, rather than implementation details. Supports outcome-focused checks without requiring a particular browser tool or automation for this competency.

sources.title: Create a verification skill
sources.note: Its Evidence section calls for the real user path, the action and resulting state, and relevant side effects. Its Launch and Doctor sections distinguish a usable connected environment from a merely responding process. These mechanisms support the required connection between a run and its claimed outcome.

competencies.title: Automated checks
competencies.meaning: Make relevant checks run through a reusable automatic workflow and let their actual results govern completion claims. Keep the workflow usable as the product changes, and distinguish passed, failed, blocked, and unexecuted checks.
competencies.evidence: Trace a reusable verification command, CI job, hook, or agent workflow from its actual trigger through check selection, execution on the affected revision, retained results, and the completion decision. Inspect subsequent applicable changes when present to see whether checks run without additional user intervention. Read failure, skip, and blocked states as well as success. Configuration or a standing instruction alone is insufficient; look for execution and evidence that its result controls the reported status. Examine maintenance when a relevant product or harness change exposes drift.
competencies.high: A working reusable mechanism runs the checks relevant to an observed change without a new task-specific additional user intervention, preserves their results, and permits only the completion scope those results support. A failed or unexecuted required check remains failed or unverified in the gate's outcome. The mechanism uses appropriate checks for the change; every task need not run a full E2E suite. Example: a the project change triggers its existing verification workflow, which runs the affected save-and-reopen check and records the result before completion. A harness failure blocks the verified-complete status; after repair, the workflow executes successfully again. A failure need not be invented when the observed mechanism already works.
competencies.medium: Relevant checks execute and their results are reported accurately, but repeated execution still depends on task-specific additional user interventions or manual reassembly, or an observed automatic workflow omits an identified required check. Example: the project's save-and-reopen run is thorough each time the person asks for it, but the next applicable change needs the same additional user intervention. The real run can be High in workflow verification while this repeatability practice remains Medium.
competencies.low: Observed work proceeds with an unsupported verified-complete status despite a failed, skipped, stale, or unexecuted required check, or knowingly continues relying on a broken recurring verification mechanism. Example: the project's job skips persistence after its setup breaks, yet its green wrapper is repeatedly used to claim that rescheduling is verified. An unavailable service accurately marked unverified is not this behavior.
competencies.whyItHelps: A functioning default workflow carries verification into the next relevant change without relying on someone remembering the same request. Connecting its real result to the completion status prevents a skipped check or an old success from being presented as current proof. Maintaining the workflow preserves that connection when the application changes.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when verification needs to recur across changes, releases, or repeated deliveries. Existing or adapted CI, hooks, scripts, and executable agent workflows count; the person need not write a new framework. High requires observed working automatic execution and result handling, not the mere presence of automation. If no comparable later change occurs, do not invent one: an observed trigger and its gate can establish current operation, while later reuse remains unobserved. A fully observed additional user intervention-dependent check can establish Medium even if an automatic trigger or gate is unverified; state that extension as a limit. Human approval of a genuine release decision does not weaken an otherwise automatic verification mechanism.

sources.title: Verification Before Completion
sources.note: The gate identifies the command supporting a claim, executes it, reads the actual output and exit status, and reports only the supported status. Supports honest completion gates; the source's instruction alone does not prove that a project has automated or followed the gate.

sources.title: Create a verification skill
sources.note: Generates a project-specific launch, drive, evidence, and cleanup procedure and requires an actual end-to-end proof before handing it over. Supports a reusable verified procedure rather than treating a newly written skill as a working mechanism.

sources.title: Maintain a verification skill
sources.note: Rechecks the feature map against source and live behavior, distinguishes harness drift from product regressions, and reports clean, changed, or blocked outcomes. Supports maintenance tied to observed behavior; its particular agent arrangement is not a scoring requirement.

competencies.title: AI output evaluation
competencies.meaning: Use a reusable evaluation system that connects representative inputs, task-specific criteria or scorers, recorded actual outputs, and comparable quality results to adoption and regression decisions for an AI-dependent feature.
competencies.evidence: Inspect the retained cases and why they represent intended use, the success criteria and grading method, the tested prompt/model/system versions, actual generated outputs, per-case judgments, and the comparison that informed acceptance or revision. Check known failures and relevant ambiguous or negative cases when the work calls for them. Read grader disagreements or suspect passes when they arise. Follow a relevant later change into a rerun when such an opportunity exists. Existing evaluation products, adapted harnesses, and delegated evaluators are valid evidence when they actually execute and retain these connections.
competencies.high: Runs a repeatable case set suited to the feature's intended use; scores the actual system outputs against clear, relevant criteria; and compares a candidate with the baseline or retained reference under comparable conditions. The recorded decision addresses material regressions as well as improvements. Known failures become retained cases when relevant; output variability or questionable grading is investigated when it could change the decision. Human, code, and model graders can all qualify when fit for the requirement. Example: the project evaluates both answerable policy questions and questions with missing eligibility facts. The same cases run against the old and revised assistant; stored replies and grades distinguish grounded answers from invented eligibility, and an unresolved invention prevents adopting the candidate under the stated rule.
competencies.medium: Evaluates actual AI outputs with useful criteria but leaves a material part of the repeatable comparison unresolved, such as representative coverage, reliable grading, comparable runs, or disposition of a visible regression. Example: the project stores and scores both versions' replies, but selects the higher total despite a report showing invented eligibility, without establishing whether that regression violates its acceptance rule. A one-off inspected answer can be useful verification without yet establishing this evaluation system.
competencies.low: Observed AI quality work accepts a version based on prompt wording, field presence, confidence, or an irrelevant aggregate while treating that as evidence of output quality, or knowingly retains a scorer that rewards a demonstrated failure. Example: the project labels a revised assistant accurate because its prompt contains a Grounding heading, while no evaluated output supports that claim.
competencies.whyItHelps: A stable case set and explicit criteria make quality changes inspectable across versions. Retaining the actual outputs explains a score and helps distinguish a model failure from a grading error. Comparable runs and regression decisions prevent an apparent aggregate improvement from hiding a failure that matters to the feature.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the work develops, changes, or assesses the quality of AI-generated answers, recommendations, decisions, or other AI-dependent behavior. Using AI to write ordinary software does not by itself create an AI-output-evaluation opportunity. If actual output evaluation fully establishes Medium, retain Medium and identify the unverified extension toward High separately. No new tool, fixed dataset size, human-written harness, optimization framework, or personal grading is required. Repeated trials are warranted when variability could alter the conclusion, rather than as a fixed quota. A later rerun is required only when a relevant later change is observed.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
sources.note: Defines tasks, trials, graders, and outcomes; recommends balanced real-use cases, stable isolated environments, grading the produced result, inspecting transcripts and grades, and maintaining regression coverage. Supports the connected evaluation system and investigation of grading failures; its illustrative dataset sizes are not rubric thresholds.

sources.title: Evaluation best practices
sources.note: Connects evaluation objectives, datasets, metrics, executed comparisons, and continuous evaluation. Recommends task-specific cases and calibrating automated scoring with human feedback. Supports comparable quality decisions without requiring OpenAI's evaluation service or adopting its example metric thresholds.

boundaries: There are exactly three competencies: real workflow verification; automatic repeated verification with honest completion gates; and a repeatable AI output evaluation system. The same run may supply evidence for distinct questions, but it does not create extra competencies or duplicate credit for the same practice.

Planning establishes the intended outcome and completion criterion. This dimension asks what executed evidence establishes about that outcome. Unit, integration, static, or mocked checks can support a scoped conclusion; they cannot establish a real workflow they never exercise.

The first competency can be High through effective manual verification. The second requires a working automatic repeated mechanism at High. The third concerns representative cases, meaningful grading, actual outputs, and comparison decisions; it is not triggered merely because AI helped implement the product.

Feedback Loops assesses how a result chooses the next attempt, repair, stop, or escalation. This dimension assesses the check's reach and validity, repeated execution, and the evidence allowed to support completion. Human Steering assesses the person's use of evidence to judge proposals, redirect work, or reconsider earlier decisions; valid automatic or delegated verification does not establish that personal judgment.

Tool Integration assesses whether a reusable tool procedure is executable and usable. Context Engineering assesses how project instructions are supplied. Their presence does not establish that verification ran or that its result controlled completion here.

Judge recorded behavior, not test counts, coverage totals, tool brands, framework installation, or asserted success. A detected failure can demonstrate effective verification. A blocked run does not establish the blocked behavior. Do not invent failures, additional sessions, or unrelated risk cases to demand more activity.

Use connected work and its observed outcomes to judge the practice qualitatively. This category adds no thresholds beyond the shared aggregation policy, project quotas, incident requirements, or statistical claims.

example.notice: Illustrative output example, not evidence from this assessment.
example.summary: You checked that an appointment stayed saved after closing and reopening the app, and the existing workflow repeated that check before reporting completion. You also compared two AI versions on the same support requests and found a reply that invented an eligibility condition.
example.expanded: Playwright's user-visible-behavior guidance supports checking what the user can actually rely on: the project's save-and-reopen observation establishes persistence. The pstack verification procedures and Superpowers completion gate support a reusable run whose evidence controls the claim, while their installation alone would establish neither. Anthropic and OpenAI's evaluation guidance connects representative cases and grading to recorded comparisons: the project has useful executed evidence, but its unresolved eligibility regression limits the quality decision.

competencies.title: AI proposal review
competencies.meaning: Examine the facts, alternatives, and consequences relevant to a consequential AI proposal, then use that understanding to accept, modify, or reject it. The person may delegate investigation and comparison to AI; assess how the returned information informs their decision.
competencies.evidence: Trace the proposal through the information the person actually considered, their decision and its basis, and the work that followed. Useful evidence includes comparisons, concrete examples, inspected outputs, relevant project constraints, and explanations checked against available facts. A requested comparison alone does not establish that its contents informed a choice. Read brief approvals in context: a short acceptance can express a supported decision when the preceding exchange establishes its basis.
competencies.high: The person examines the information that could materially change the choice, makes a decision supported by that information, and reviews whether the resulting work follows it. Accepting a sound AI proposal meets the same standard as rejecting one. Example: AI proposes removing email verification to reduce signup abandonment. The person asks AI to inspect where abandonment occurs and explain the account-recovery consequences. The findings locate most abandonment before verification. The person retains verification, chooses to simplify the earlier form, and examines the revised signup flow to confirm both parts of that decision.
competencies.medium: Relevant information informs an identifiable decision, but a consequential implication remains unresolved or the connection to subsequent work is unconfirmed. Example: the person compares two signup approaches and chooses the simpler one for a stated usability reason, but leaves the account-recovery problem raised in the comparison unresolved.
competencies.low: A consequential proposal calls for a decision, but the person proceeds without examining the material implications or chooses for a reason that disregards the available findings. Example: AI presents a migration choice that affects existing customer records, and the person says, "Pick anything and proceed," without considering that consequence. Another example is choosing the replacement solely because it is newer after the comparison identifies an unresolved data-loss risk.
competencies.whyItHelps: Separating fact-finding from decision-making lets AI supply information the person does not already know while keeping the choice connected to the person's objectives. Examining the material implications can expose a persuasive proposal that solves the wrong problem or creates an unacceptable consequence. A supported acceptance also lets suitable work proceed without unnecessary intervention.
competencies.applicability: Applies when a proposal presents a material choice about the intended outcome, approach, or consequences. Routine execution within an already established decision does not require another comparison or approval. Assess the information needed for the actual choice; do not require multiple alternatives when the available evidence already supports one suitable approach.

sources.title: Matt Pocock skills — Grilling
sources.note: Separates facts the agent should investigate from decisions presented to the person, and uses successive answers to resolve dependent choices. Adopted mechanism: delegate discoverable facts while connecting consequential choices to the person's considered answers. The skill's interview format and confirmation procedure are not scoring requirements.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit — Guideline 11: Make clear why the system did what it did
sources.note: Recommends accessible explanations while warning that an explanation's presence can increase trust and overreliance even when AI is wrong. Adopted mechanism: examine whether the available explanation and evidence support the choice rather than treating receipt of an explanation as informed judgment. This is interaction-design guidance, not validation of the behavioral levels.

competencies.title: AI work correction
competencies.meaning: When AI work departs from the intended result, follows an unsupported explanation, or expands beyond a justified scope, identify the mismatch, communicate an actionable correction, and judge whether the subsequent work addresses it.
competencies.evidence: Follow the disputed proposal or observed result through the evidence the person considered, their correction, AI's response, and the person's judgment of the returned work. Inspect relevant outputs, screen states, diffs, reproductions, or explanations of competing causes. Determine what the correction changes and what it preserves. The person may ask AI to investigate the cause rather than identify the implementation themselves.
competencies.high: The person connects the correction to the observed problem, gives a usable change of direction or scope, and examines subsequent evidence to judge whether the original need and correction were addressed. Example: asked to export copies, AI starts moving the source files. The person explains that the goal is delivery rather than relocation, directs AI to preserve the originals and create separate exports, and inspects both the exported files and the retained originals before accepting the result.
competencies.medium: The person identifies a concrete mismatch and gives a correction AI can apply, but the evidence supporting the chosen direction or the person's judgment of its effect remains incomplete. Example: "Exporting removes the originals. Preserve them and create copies instead." This is an actionable correction, but the subsequent record does not show the person inspecting whether the originals remain.
competencies.low: An observed mismatch calls for correction, but the person provides no usable change or directs work that does not address the demonstrated problem. Example: after seeing that export removes the originals, the person repeatedly says only "Try again," or asks AI to rename the export button while leaving the file-moving behavior unaddressed.
competencies.whyItHelps: An unexplained retry can preserve the same mistaken assumption. A correction tied to evidence changes what AI investigates or implements, while explicit preservation conditions protect the parts that should remain. Reviewing the returned result distinguishes a resolved problem from an appealing explanation or an unrelated improvement.
competencies.applicability: Applies when a proposed or ongoing approach creates a concrete mismatch, unsupported direction, or unjustified scope. Correct autonomous work need not be interrupted to demonstrate this competency. A request to change direction may appropriately begin with further investigation rather than a prescribed fix.

sources.title: pstack — Poteto mode: Bug fix playbook
sources.note: Requires runtime evidence to discriminate causes, removal of changes motivated by refuted hypotheses, and verification on the original surface. Adopted mechanism: reject an unsupported direction for an evidenced reason, constrain the replacement to the demonstrated problem, and examine the original outcome afterward. The playbook addresses agent execution; its delegation and commit procedures are not requirements for human steering.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit — Guideline 9: Support efficient correction
sources.note: Recommends letting people edit, refine, or recover from incorrect AI output, including adjusting part of a proposed route using local knowledge. Adopted mechanism: a focused correction can preserve useful work while addressing the specific mismatch. The guideline supports correction as an interaction mechanism rather than prescribing these assessment levels.

competencies.title: Assumption checks
competencies.meaning: Reconsider an earlier instruction, assumption, or choice when new findings challenge its basis. Use the evidence to revise or deliberately retain the decision, then examine the resulting work.
competencies.evidence: Identify the person's earlier position, the finding that challenges it, their interpretation of that finding, the decision they revise or retain, and the subsequent result. Distinguish reconsideration of an existing assumption from an ordinary new preference or added requirement. AI disagreement alone is insufficient; inspect the supporting evidence and how the person uses it.
competencies.high: The person examines what the new evidence changes about their earlier reasoning, revises or retains the decision for a supported reason, and reviews the resulting work. Example: the person requests more help articles to reduce support inquiries. User observations then show that the needed explanations already exist but are difficult to find. The person revises the assumption that more content is needed, directs AI to expose the existing explanation at the relevant step, and examines whether the revised flow lets people find it and complete the task. Retaining an earlier choice also qualifies when the person addresses the contrary finding and the evidence supports that choice.
competencies.medium: The person recognizes the conflict and makes a relevant revision or retention decision, but part of its reasoning or subsequent effect remains unconfirmed. Example: after reviewing the discoverability finding, the person replaces the article-writing request with an in-context help link, but no later observation establishes how the revised flow works.
competencies.low: Evidence challenges an earlier decision, but the person refuses to examine it or revises or retains the decision for a reason that does not address the finding. Example: after receiving the existing articles and observations showing that people cannot find them, the person insists, "Ignore that and write the extra articles I originally requested," or asks for longer articles without addressing discoverability.
competencies.whyItHelps: Correct execution cannot compensate for a mistaken premise in the instruction itself. Testing the premise behind an earlier decision can prevent further work on an explanation the evidence no longer supports. Deliberate retention is equally useful when examination shows that the original decision remains appropriate; changing one's mind is not the objective.
competencies.applicability: Applies when a finding challenges an identifiable earlier instruction or assumption. Neither a reversal nor repeated failure is required. Examine whether the person addresses the challenge; a supported decision to retain the original direction can demonstrate the same practice.

sources.title: pstack — Attack the Premise
sources.note: Calls for stating and directly testing a premise when fixes that share it fail, then following evidence that confirms or contradicts it. Adopted mechanism: examine the assumption behind a direction before continuing to invest in it. This rubric extends that mechanism to the person's own instructions and choices; the source's repeated-failure trigger is not adopted as a prerequisite.

boundaries: Distinguish the decision being assessed: choosing among proposals, correcting AI's approach, and reconsidering the person's own earlier position. One episode can support more than one competency only when it contains distinguishable decisions and evidence for each. Do not award three credits for one correction described in different words.

Planning & Specs establishes the initial intended outcome and working conditions. Testing & Evals assesses what checks establish. Feedback Loops assesses how results control execution. Human Steering assesses the person's decisions when considering proposals, correcting the approach, or reconsidering their own position.

example.notice: Illustrative output example, not evidence from this assessment.
example.summary: In the project, you explained why moving the source files did not meet the export request and directed AI to preserve the originals. You then inspected the exported copies and retained originals before accepting the result.
example.expanded: The pstack bug-fix playbook connects a changed direction to observed evidence and checks the original outcome after repair; Microsoft HAX Guideline 9 supports focused correction using the person's local knowledge. Here, the mismatch informed an actionable correction and the person's later inspection supported acceptance. This demonstrates redirection; proposal decisions and reconsideration of an earlier personal assumption require their own identifiable decisions.

competencies.title: Access control
competencies.meaning: Match an AI task's access to its authorized actors, resources, and operations, then enforce that boundary where an action takes effect. This includes the working agent's access and protected operations it changes in a product, when each is relevant.
competencies.evidence: Connect the task's authorization to the identity, resource, operation, and effective control used during execution. Inspect credential scopes, service authorization, sandbox or approval decisions, relevant code paths, and actual allow/deny results. A written rule, an installed tool, or an uneventful run alone does not demonstrate enforcement; a product sandbox does not establish restrictions on the working agent.
competencies.high: The needed operation succeeds and a relevant unauthorized operation is demonstrably denied at the applicable enforcement point. Discovered gaps are fixed and the affected checks rerun. Example: the project's reporting agent reads fixture invoices with its scoped identity, while an attempted fixture deletion is denied; a changed invoice endpoint also permits its owner and denies another account. Existing controls earn credit when their application and result are observed.
competencies.medium: A specific suitable control is applied to the actual operation, but its relevant allow/deny behavior is not fully established. Example: the project runs the report with a verified read-only database role and retrieves the requested data, but has not checked the role against a safe write attempt. A promise to ask before changes is insufficient without an applied approval or access mechanism.
competencies.low: Records establish that a required authorization boundary is absent or violated and the task ends without correcting it. Example: the project's changed endpoint returns another account's fixture invoice through a confirmed missing ownership check, and that exposure remains unresolved. State the demonstrated exposure without inventing subsequent harm.
competencies.whyItHelps: Enforcement ties authority to a concrete operation even if an agent makes a mistake. Checking both permitted and denied cases distinguishes a useful restriction from one that either grants too much or prevents legitimate work.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when AI work accesses protected resources, performs consequential actions, or changes protected product operations. Assess only boundaries relevant to that task; safe fixtures can demonstrate prevention without an incident. A permissive agent setting alone proves neither unnecessary access nor absence of other controls. Human approval is appropriate at a genuine authorization boundary, and the human need not implement the control personally.

sources.title: OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Maps actors, resources, and operations to least privilege; recommends permission checks on each protected request and tests of their enforcement. Supports the task-specific access boundary and allowed/denied comparison.

sources.title: Anthropic: Beyond permission prompts: making Claude Code more secure and autonomous
sources.note: Describes filesystem and network isolation enforced outside model judgment, including subprocesses. Supports inspecting effective agent restrictions while preserving ordinary work; no particular sandbox product or published performance claim is required.

sources.title: pstack: Prove It Works (skills/principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Requires checking the actual artifact or behavior rather than a proxy or self-report. Adopted only as an evidence principle for observed control outcomes, not as a security guarantee.

competencies.title: Sensitive data protection
competencies.meaning: Limit secrets and sensitive information to the data, recipients, destinations, and retention the task permits. Apply protection to the relevant path through tools, model context, outputs, logs, and saved artifacts rather than relying on a general warning.
competencies.evidence: Trace what information was needed, its permitted use, and where it actually traveled or was stored. Read scoped retrieval, secret injection, field filtering or redaction, outbound restrictions, relevant diffs and logs, and safe disclosure checks. Distinguish a real value exposed to an unauthorized destination from a synthetic test value, and inspect containment or credential revocation when an exposure occurred.
competencies.high: The required task completes with the permitted data, while a safe check shows a relevant prohibited disclosure is blocked, removed, or kept inaccessible at the boundary. Any observed exposure is contained and the affected path checked again. Example: the project's support summary retains the issue details it needs, but seeded private identifiers are removed before the external model request; the recorded request verifies both results without using real personal data.
competencies.medium: A specific suitable protection operates on the actual data path, but disclosure verification is incomplete. Example: the project's export passes through an applied field allowlist before the AI receives it, but no seeded private-field case has been checked at that outbound boundary. An unused secret scanner or an instruction saying not to leak data is insufficient.
competencies.low: A required information boundary is demonstrably missing or violated and remains uncorrected. Example: a live token is observed in the project's public patch or an unauthorized outbound payload, and the task finishes without containment and credential invalidation. Missing logs, unavailable vendor settings, or the mere presence of credentials in the environment do not establish this failure.
competencies.whyItHelps: Reducing the sensitive information available to a process and controlling its destinations reduces opportunities for accidental disclosure. Checking the actual outbound or saved artifact catches leaks that a clean final message can conceal.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the task handles secrets, private records, confidential material, or a path that could expose them. Use synthetic markers or fixtures for checks; never require disclosure of real secrets as proof. Proper use of an approved connector or secret store counts when the observed path preserves the boundary; asking the user to paste the secret is unnecessary.

sources.title: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Recommends fine-grained secret access, minimizing direct handling, lifecycle controls, and revocation of potentially compromised secrets. Supports protecting the necessary credential path and addressing confirmed exposure.

sources.title: OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
sources.note: Identifies confidential information and credentials as disclosure risks and describes restricted data access, sanitization, and redaction. Notes that prompt restrictions may be bypassed; supports checking the data path rather than trusting instructions alone.

sources.title: Addy Osmani agent-skills: Security and Hardening (skills/security-and-hardening/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Specifies secret handling outside source, removal of sensitive response fields, and keeping secrets or other tenants' data out of LLM context. Adopted for concrete handling paths, without importing its entire audit checklist.

competencies.title: External input safety
competencies.meaning: Treat fetched pages, documents, messages, tool responses, third-party skills, and model output according to who controls them. Keep their content from becoming unauthorized instructions, executable code, or unchecked tool parameters when it crosses a trust boundary.
competencies.evidence: Follow an external input from its entry channel to the action or output it can influence. Inspect separation of instructions from source data, boundary parsing and validation, safe rendering or command construction, permission checks on tool calls, and observed results with benign and adversarial fixtures. A refusal in the answer is insufficient if a tool already performed the forbidden action.
competencies.high: The intended external-content task succeeds, and a relevant malicious or malformed fixture fails to cross the protected boundary. The check uses the same input channel and observes the tool call, destination, or state at risk; discovered gaps are repaired and checked again. Example: the project summarizes a retrieved page normally, while an embedded instruction to send a dummy private record to a test destination produces no outbound call because the tool policy denies that destination.
competencies.medium: A specific defense is applied to the actual boundary, but its relevant adversarial behavior remains unverified. Example: the project parses an imported action into an allowlisted schema and checks the target against session permissions, but has tested only a normal import. A prompt to ignore malicious instructions, with no observed handling or downstream control, does not establish this level.
competencies.low: Records demonstrate an uncorrected required boundary failure. Example: an imported document's embedded instruction is followed into an unauthorized tool call, or attacker-controlled input is confirmed to reach a shell command without the required safe construction. A suspicious document alone, an untested scanner warning, or no attack record does not establish a violation.
competencies.whyItHelps: Separating data from authority prevents an outside author from acquiring the user's permissions merely by supplying content. Validation and downstream action controls address different failure paths; observing the actual protected effect avoids confusing a polite refusal with prevention.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when externally controlled content can influence AI instructions, executable behavior, tool parameters, or security-sensitive output. Choose checks for the actual input channel and consequence; a passing fixture establishes only that tested protection, not universal prompt-injection resistance. Existing parsers, tool policies, and framework escaping count when appropriately used and observed.

sources.title: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sources.note: Explains indirect injection through external sources and recommends separating external content, validating outputs, and restricting privileges in code. Supports distinguishing supplied content from authority.

sources.title: OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Recommends validating tool parameters against permissions and session context. Its smoke-testing section uses dummy data, the actual external channel, observable tool or disclosure outcomes, and legitimate controls; it explicitly limits what passing cases prove.

sources.title: pstack: Boundary Discipline (skills/principle-boundary-discipline/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Places parsing, validation, and defensive error handling at external boundaries. Adopted as a supporting implementation mechanism; parsed or typed data still requires authorization and safe use.

sources.title: Addy Osmani agent-skills: Security and Hardening (skills/security-and-hardening/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Treats model output and externally written values as untrusted, requires safe query/command/output handling, and distinguishes valid shape from authorized use. Supports tracing the input to its dangerous sink.

boundaries: Security assesses protections relevant to the observed AI task, including applicable protections in its output. It does not require an exhaustive repository audit, every scanner, a real incident, or a fixed control count.

Authorization concerns who may act on which resource. Sensitive information concerns what may be retrieved, disclosed, or retained. External input concerns whether an outside source can gain authority or reach a dangerous sink. One connected case can inform these distinct questions without inventing extra incidents.

Testing & Evals owns general workflow verification and reusable evaluation systems; Security owns whether the relevant protection permits the intended case and prevents the prohibited case. Human Steering assesses the person's substantive judgment of proposals, corrections, and earlier decisions; a security approval alone does not establish that judgment.

Boundary parsing, types, idempotency, and direct proof can support a particular protection; none alone proves security. A clean scan, successful build, saved configuration, tool installation, or permissive setting is not a substitute for connected evidence. No separate permission-bypass deduction is added.

example.notice: Illustrative output example, not evidence from this assessment.
example.summary: In the project's invoice report, your scoped agent completed the permitted query and a safe deletion attempt was denied. In the project's importer, the schema and session checks were applied, but the record does not yet show an embedded instruction being stopped at the outbound tool boundary.
example.expanded: OWASP's authorization guidance links actors and operations to enforced permissions, so the project's observed query and denial support High for that task's authorization boundary. OWASP's injection guidance requires observing the protected action through the relevant external channel; the project's applied controls support Medium while that verification is incomplete. These observations say nothing about unobserved sensitive-information paths or the projects' overall security.

competencies.title: Model and effort selection
competencies.meaning: Choose and actually use a model and reasoning effort suited to the work's difficulty, required quality, urgency, and likely correction burden. Assess the main run and delegated work when delegation occurs.
competencies.evidence: Connect the task's acceptance conditions to the person's choice, an adopted AI proposal, or an applied standing rule; then inspect resolved execution settings, delivered behavior, verification, and repairs. Look for both model capability and reasoning effort where the platform allows them to be selected or observed. A requested setting is not proof of the setting that ran. Defaults can be deliberate choices when the records show why they fit. Do not require the person to research facts or choose every subagent manually when an authorized AI can do that work.
competencies.high: A task-specific choice of model and effort governs the actual execution, and observed completion checks establish that the assignment delivered the required result. The choice accounts for difficulty and correction risk rather than price or model reputation alone. Example: for a bounded internal rename, an adopted rule selects the ordinary coding model at medium effort; the resolved run uses that assignment and passes the reference checks. An interacting authorization change receives a more capable model or higher effort because its cases cross several rules, and the executed checks cover those cases. One model can fit both tasks if the evidence supports that choice.
competencies.medium: Makes and applies a concrete resource choice but handles a relevant part of task fit incompletely. Example: an import repair runs on the selected lower-cost model, but the recorded selection considers only request price even though the known requirement includes ambiguous mappings and previous correction work. Or execution reports a fallback model, yet the task review still attributes the result to the requested model without resolving the difference. This is an observed partial practice, not a rating for absent metadata.
competencies.low: Continues an assignment after inspected results establish that it misses the required behavior, or adds resource use whose redundancy is already demonstrated, without addressing that mismatch. Example: the same effort setting repeatedly misses the documented permission interaction; the person keeps requesting the same attempt despite the failed cases and recurring repair, with no revised assignment or execution approach. A costly successful run or a failed first attempt alone does not establish Low.
competencies.whyItHelps: Capability and reasoning effort affect what a run can resolve, how long it takes, and how much correction follows. Matching both to the actual task can avoid unnecessary work while preserving the result the person needs. Confirming what ran prevents a setting request from becoming a false explanation of the outcome.
competencies.applicability: Applicable whenever AI performs a task with a resource assignment to assess, including small one-off tasks. A concrete applied choice with the observed incomplete task-fit judgment described at Medium remains Medium, even if its final effect is unverified; state that limit separately. If effort is unavailable or not exposed, state that limit and assess the supported choices without inventing hidden settings or treating unavailable telemetry as a personal failure.

sources.title: OpenAI API — Reasoning models, Reasoning effort
sources.note: Explains the effort control and its quality, latency, and token tradeoffs; supported settings depend on the model. This supports assessing effort alongside model choice rather than using a model name as the entire assignment. It does not establish a suitable effort for an unobserved task.

sources.title: pstack — skills/poteto-mode/SKILL.md, Subagents
sources.note: The public procedure starts from per-role settings, adjusts reasoning effort for task difficulty, and distinguishes difficult changes from mechanical edits. Adopt the task-based selection mechanism, not its named model defaults or a requirement to use subagents.

competencies.title: Quality and total effort
competencies.meaning: Judge resource use against the accepted result and everything needed to reach it: execution, verification, failed attempts, retries, coordination, and human review or repair. Use that evidence to decide whether the approach is worth retaining or changing.
competencies.evidence: Read the required result, actual outputs and checks, attempt history, usage by the main run and any delegates, available timing, and records of human checking or correction. Connect the accounting scope to the conclusion. Distinguish observed elapsed time from active work time, API price estimates from actual charges, and subscription allowance from monetary spend. When alternatives are compared, require comparable task scope, inputs, and completion checks, and include unsuccessful attempts rather than only the best run.
competencies.high: Reviews achieved quality with the whole observable completion burden, identifies unavailable quantities explicitly, and uses the result to justify retaining or changing the approach. Example: a report for the project includes a failed mapping attempt, the repair, delegated inspection, final checks, and the person's review work. It shows that the apparent saving on the first request was offset by repair and retains the route that meets the mapping cases with the better supported overall tradeoff. If billing or active work time is unavailable, the report identifies those quantities as unavailable and makes its conclusion only from the supported usage, timing, and correction evidence. A well-supported decision to retain an effective existing assignment also qualifies.
competencies.medium: Connects a real result to real resource evidence but omits or mislabels a known contributor, so the conclusion covers only part of the work. Example: a comparison includes passing output and final-call usage but leaves recorded retries and human repair outside the total. Or it labels an API-price estimate as the subscription charge. The observed accounting is useful but does not yet support its stated whole-task conclusion.
competencies.low: Selects or calls an approach efficient while inspected evidence contradicts its required result or hides the repair needed to obtain it. Example: the lower-token import run is adopted as the efficient option even though it fails the required mapping cases, and the separately recorded repair run is excluded after that problem is pointed out. Large totals, long sessions, or unavailable billing alone do not establish waste.
competencies.whyItHelps: A request uses resources even when its output is discarded. Counting the work needed for an acceptable completion makes retries, handoffs, and human repair visible instead of rewarding an inexpensive unsuccessful attempt. Comparable completion conditions make a resource difference interpretable.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when there is an observed execution episode whose quality and resource burden can be reviewed, or a decision comparing approaches. Do not demand new benchmark runs merely to manufacture a comparison, invent human review minutes from message gaps, or convert session wall time into active labor.

sources.title: Efficient Agents: Building Effective Agents While Reducing Cost — Section 2.2 Metrics
sources.note: Separates input and output costs and uses cost-of-pass to relate cost to successful completion. Adopt the comparison principle that cost and success must be read together; the rubric additionally considers observed time and human repair. The paper's benchmark figures do not predict savings for a person's projects.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents, When (and when not) to use agents
sources.note: Recommends starting with a simple solution and considering whether added agent complexity earns its latency and cost through better task performance. This supports evaluating orchestration overhead against the required result, without rewarding or penalizing an agent count by itself.

competencies.title: Automatic model selection
competencies.meaning: Turn useful quality-and-resource findings into maintained selection rules that the AI or harness applies to new tasks. The person's own standing rule can classify task size or difficulty and select model, effort, or justified delegation; a separate router product is not required.
competencies.evidence: Trace a reviewed result to a retained or revised assignment rule, then to a later relevant task that consumes it and the resolved settings that actually run. Inspect how the rule reaches the execution path: automatically loaded instructions that the AI applies, a reusable workflow, per-role configuration, or a router. Check the later result and resource burden against the reason for the rule. Distinguish an automatically applied standing policy from a file that is never read, a requested route that resolves differently, or the person repeating a model instruction on each task.
competencies.high: A maintained rule grounded in reviewed outcomes automatically governs a later applicable assignment without the person restating the routine selection, and the later result supports retaining or revising it. Example: a standing workflow classifies isolated edits separately from changes with interacting access rules, chooses the model and effort for that class, and verifies the resolved assignment. A later access-rule repair receives the intended route without additional user intervention; its checks and total attempt burden are reviewed. If those results show a changed requirement or recurring mismatch, the rule is revised and the next applicable execution follows it. Deliberately keeping a successful route qualifies. Genuine preference or risk decisions can still require human approval.
competencies.medium: Uses an evidence-based reusable selection criterion, but the observed execution still needs a human additional user intervention for routine routing or leaves a known gap between the rule and its purpose. Example: the person has a useful task-size rule yet must repeat the appropriate model and effort on each comparable task. Or the later run automatically selects the intended settings but the recorded review considers only price despite the rule having been introduced to reduce correction work.
competencies.low: Leaves an established recurring resource or quality problem in place after reviewing it and adopting a relevant lesson, despite a later opportunity to apply that lesson. Example: reviews identify that the default route causes repeated mapping repairs, but later comparable tasks continue through the unchanged default and the person still labels the saved, unused policy an improvement. Having no commercial router, using one model, or overriding a route for a justified exception does not establish Low.
competencies.whyItHelps: An applied standing rule carries a useful decision into the next task and removes repeated routine selection from the person. Connecting the rule to resolved settings exposes configuration drift. Reviewing later outcomes keeps the rule tied to its purpose as tasks and available models change.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when assignment decisions recur or the work has a reusable routing need. Credit delegated or automatic routing only when its operation is observed. Human judgment on a new substantive decision need not be automated.

sources.title: pstack — skills/setup-pstack/SKILL.md
sources.note: Writes persistent per-role model and budget settings, validates available model identifiers, and explains how later skills consume the settings in each harness. This supplies a concrete reusable-policy mechanism; the rubric still requires observed later execution rather than credit for the settings file alone.

sources.title: pstack — skills/poteto-mode/SKILL.md, Match the model to the job
sources.note: Applies saved role settings at dispatch and adjusts effort to the job. This supports automatic task-based selection under a person's standing policy. Its specific defaults are examples, not universal efficiency targets.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents, Workflow: Routing
sources.note: Describes classifying inputs and directing them to appropriate paths, including model choices for distinct task classes. This supports routing by observed task needs, without requiring multiple models when one route fits the work.

boundaries: Assess the fit and effect of resources, not prestige, list price, subscription tier, model variety, or agent count. A premium model, inexpensive model, one model, or several agents can each be appropriate.

Task Mapping assesses useful work units, ownership, handoff, and integration. This dimension assesses the model, reasoning effort, and resource burden of executing those units; the same delegation event earns no automatic efficiency credit.

Testing & Evals establishes whether the result meets its quality conditions. This dimension connects that quality to total resources and assignment decisions. Merely rerunning a check is not a separate efficiency competency.

Feedback Loops assesses how results guide progress and repairs. This dimension examines whether retries and repairs justify a resource choice and inform a maintained assignment rule; a failed attempt is not itself inefficiency.

Credit an AI's appropriate assignment under the person's adopted policy when its actual operation is observed. Do not require the person to choose every model manually, and do not attribute an unaided AI decision to the person's personal reasoning.

Keep token categories, monetary charges, API estimates, subscription usage, elapsed time, active work, and human review distinct. Report unavailable quantities explicitly and make no unsupported savings or labor claims.

Automation is required for High in reusable resource routing, through an applied workflow, harness behavior, or instructions the AI consumes and follows. A commercial router, multiple models, extra agents, and automation of personal judgment are not required.

example.summary: In the project, you compared accepted mapping behavior with the failed attempt, repair, and review before retaining the more suitable route. Your standing task-size rule then selected the intended model and effort for a later import change without another model-selection additional user intervention, and the follow-up review checked that the reason for the rule still held.
example.expanded: The public routing sources supply two mechanisms: a persistent assignment map and a workflow that applies it to the incoming task. The illustrative observation connects those mechanisms to an actual later assignment and its result, so it supports reusable routing rather than merely proving that a policy file exists. The whole-task review also follows the cost-and-success comparison principle, while identifying monetary spend as unavailable when billing is unavailable.
